parole.significato: abbreviation (shortened or contracted form of a word or phrase)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin abbreviātiōnem. By surface analysis, abreviar + -ção.
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin agonia, from Ancient Greek ἀγωνία (agōnía, “emulation, competition, struggle”), from ἀγών (agṓn, “contest”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese aleluia, from Ecclesiastical Latin allelūia, from Hebrew הַלְלוּיָהּ (“Praise Yah”).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin apostatāre (“to forsake one's religion, to apostatize”), from Ancient Greek ἀποστατέω (apostatéō, “stand aloof from; fall away (from the divine)”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese arcediago, a semi-learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin archidiāconus. Doublet of arquidiácono.
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin baptistērium, from Ancient Greek βαπτιστήριον (baptistḗrion).

From Old Galician-Portuguese bautizar, batiçar, a semi-learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin baptīzāre (“to baptise”), from Ancient Greek βαπτίζω (baptízō, “to immerse, plunge, baptise”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin benedictus (“blessed”), perfect passive participle of Latin benedīcō (“to speak well of”). Doublet of bento, Bento, and Benedito.

From Old Galician-Portuguese beento, bẽeyto, from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin benedictus, perfect passive participle of Latin benedīcō (“to speak well (of)”). Doublet of bendito, a semi-learned borrowing, and Benedito.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese bẽeiçon, from beençon (which yielded benção), from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin benedictiōnem (“blessing; benediction”), from benedictus, from Latin benedīcō. The plural in -ãos was formed by analogy with other paroxytones in -ão. Doublet of bendição, a lat

parole.significato: chapter (a council or community of canons)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese cabidoo, from Ecclesiastical Latin capitulum (“ecclesiastical council or body”). Doublet of capítulo.
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin canōnizāre.
From canto (“chant”) + chão (“flat, plain”), from Ecclesiastical Latin cantus planus (“plainchant”).

parole.significato: schism (a split or separation within a group or organisation)
parole.testo: Semi-learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin schisma, from Ancient Greek σχίσμα (skhísma, “division”).
Inherited from Ecclesiastical Latin compassiōnem, from Latin compatior.
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin commūniōnem, from Latin commūnis.

parole.significato: to confess; to own up to; to admit to (to admit one has done something, especially something bad)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese confessar, from Ecclesiastical Latin cōnfessāre (“to confess”) (possibly an inheritance), a derivative of Latin cōnfessus, past participle of cōnfiteor (“to confess, to admit”) from con- + fateor (“to admit”).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin dalmatica, feminine of dalmaticus (literally “Dalmatian”), from the name of the province of Dalmatia.
From Ecclesiastical Latin degradāre, from Latin de- (“down, away from”) + gradus (“grade, step”).

parole.significato: deacon (a designated minister of charity in the early Church)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin diāconus, from Ancient Greek διᾱ́κονος (diā́konos).

Inherited from Ecclesiastical Latin incarnātus, past participle of incarnō (“to make or become incarnate; to make into flesh”), from in- + Latin carō (“flesh”). Compare archaic Spanish encarnado, Asturian encarnáu.
Inherited from Ecclesiastical Latin incarnāre, from Latin carō (“flesh”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese encarnaçon, borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin incarnātiōnem. Cognate with Galician and Spanish encarnación, Catalan encarnació, French incarnation and Italian incarnazione.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin erēmīta, from Ancient Greek ἐρημίτης (erēmítēs).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin ēvangelium, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion, “good news”).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin immāteriālis.

parole.significato: intinction (partial submersion of the host in the consecrated wine)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin intinctio, from intingere (“to dip in”); prefix in- (“in”) + tingere (“to tinge”).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin limbus (“limbo”), from Latin limbus (“border, edge”).
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin martyrologium.
From Old Galician-Portuguese missa, from Ecclesiastical Latin missa (“mass”), from Latin mittō (“to send”), from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to exchange, remove”).
From Ecclesiastical Latin martyr, from Ancient Greek μάρτυς (mártus, “witness”).
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin offuscāre (“to darken, to obscure”), from Latin ob- + fuscō (“to darken”). Compare French offusquer.
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin ōrātōrium (“place of prayer, oratory”), substantive of ōrātōrius (“oratorical”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese papa, probably borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin papas, from Ancient Greek πάπας (pápas, “bishop, patriarch”), variant of πάππας (páppas, “father”).
From Ecclesiastical Latin propāganda, short for Congregātiō dē Propagandā Fide, "congregation for propagating the faith".

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese quarta feira (“Wednesday”), from Ecclesiastical Latin quārta fēria (“Wednesday”, literally “fourth weekday”); displaced earlier mércores. Compare Galician cuarta feira and Mirandese quarta-feira.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese quinta feira (“Thursday”), from Ecclesiastical Latin quīnta fēria (“Thursday”, literally “fifth weekday”); displaced earlier joves. Compare Galician quinta feira and Mirandese quinta-feira.
From Old Galician-Portuguese sacramento, sagramento, from Ecclesiastical Latin sacrāmentum, from Latin sacrō. By surface analysis, sagrar + -mento.
From Ecclesiastical Latin sacristia, from sacer (“sacred, holy”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese segunda feira (“Monday”), from Ecclesiastical Latin secunda fēria (“Monday”, literally “second weekday”); displaced earlier lũes. Compare Galician segunda feira and Mirandese segunda-feira.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sesta feira (“Friday”), a learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin sexta fēria (“Friday”, literally “sixth weekday”), from Latin fēria + sexta, literally “sixth weekday”. displaced earlier vernes. Compare Galician sexta feira (“Friday”), Mirandese sesta-feir

parole.significato: simony (act of buying and selling ecclesiastical offices and pardons)
parole.testo: From Ecclesiastical Latin simonia (“simony”), after Simon the Sorcerer, from Hebrew שִׁמְעוֹן (Šimʻôn, “Simon”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese terça feira (“Tuesday”), from Ecclesiastical Latin tertia fēria (“Tuesday”, literally “third weekday”); displaced earlier martes. Related to Galician terza feira and Mirandese terça-feira.
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin trānsfōrmātiōnem, from Latin trānsfōrmō. By surface analysis, transformar + -ção.
